_meta.warning: Every figure below is a published estimate, not a quoted price. No microreactor has sold power commercially, so no realised LCOE exists anywhere in this table. Ranges are wide because they encode different assumptions about FOAK vs Nth-of-a-kind cost maturity — that spread IS the finding, not noise to average away.
_meta.review: Reviewed 2026-08-21 against an energy/project-finance reading. Three corrections applied: the diesel comparison was overstated (bands overlap), the at-scale case was implying a false capex sensitivity, and the PTC scenario was missing its U.S.-only scope.

microreactor_lcoe.basis: Comparable to or below diesel-based electricity in remote locations

source.label: Nuclear Business Platform — microreactor market review

microreactor_lcoe.caveat: The PTC is a U.S. federal incentive and does not apply to the international track. Any export case should be read against the unsubsidised bands.

Not a pure capex sensitivity. Halving capital cost ($5,000→$2,500/kW) drops LCOE 59% ($85→$35/MWh) — more than full pass-through, which is arithmetically impossible if capex were the only variable. The at-scale case necessarily bundles other improvements (capacity factor, O&M, fuel cycle). Treat it as a scenario, not a lever.

displaced_alternatives.note: NEI report concludes electricity from microreactors will cost less than diesel generators

reading: Read the overlaps, not the midpoints. Against **rural Alaska** ($350–600/MWh) the microreactor band ($200–330) clears cleanly — that is the one genuinely uncontested win, and it is why Fort Wainwright is the most interesting row in the Army Janus table. Against **remote diesel** ($250–400) the bands overlap: a microreactor at the top of its range ($330) still loses to diesel at the bottom of its range ($250), so 'cheaper than diesel' is a site-by-site claim that turns on local fuel logistics, not a category claim. Against grid-connected U.S. industrial power the microreactor loses badly in every published case except the PTC and at-scale scenarios, both of which are forward-looking. The commercial logic therefore inverts by sector: off-grid sites can buy on cost today, on-grid sites buy on resilience, speed-to-power or carbon and pay a premium to do it.
